case_study_insert.main_stem: Lakeside Escape Inns (LEI) is a public limited company in the hospitality and hotel sector, running boutique inns and lakeside cabins and employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2015 by Naledi Khan, LEI uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership, giving experienced inn managers freedom over local decisions. It plans to invest $720,000 in two new cabins and a spa, financed by a $400,000 share issue and a $320,000 five-year bank loan. LEI has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $30.00 a unit and a selling price of $55.00, and currently produces 18,000 units a year, each unit being one guest-room night. Recently cleanliness complaints have risen to 34 a month and housekeeping staff turnover is high, worrying managers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Guest and Quality Report — Q3 2025: LEI sold 4,800 room-nights at $55.00 each, with an occupancy rate of 78%. Cleanliness complaints rose from 18 to 34 per month, and the 2025 guest survey found 72% of 380 respondents would return and 63% rated the lakeside location as the main reason for booking. Average check-in time is 12 minutes. Retraining a housekeeping employee costs $540.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Lakeside Escape Inns as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Hospitality Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.75%, increasing costs on LEI's $320,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.20 to $14.04 per hour from April 2026, raising the housekeeping wage bill. (3) Energy and laundry input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year while hospitality inflation is 5.6%, and domestic weekend breaks grew 4.8%.

questions.question_text: LEI is funding its new cabins and spa partly with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for LEI of using a share issue instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $400,000 share issue raises equity that needs no interest or capital repayment, easing pressure on cash flow while LEI already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $320,000 loan. The money saved can be spent on the $540 housekeeping retraining needed to cut the 34 monthly cleanliness complaints, protecting the $55.00 room price and the $25.00 earned on each guest-room night.

Point 2: Equity does not have to be secured against the company's assets, so the new cabins and spa cannot be repossessed if occupancy slips below the current 78%. As a public limited company, Naledi Khan can also spread risk among many shareholders rather than committing the 52-strong workforce to another fixed debt obligation; unlike a loan, dividends can be reduced in a weak year, giving LEI flexibility while it builds the new accommodation. Unlike a fixed loan repayment, a dividend on the $400,000 share issue can be lowered when 78% occupancy falls, protecting the 52 staff and the $720,000 project. Equity therefore gives LEI more resilience than debt if the 6.4% wage rise and 10.2% energy inflation squeeze margins.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to LEI, its share issue and its hotel operations.

questions.question_text: LEI is promoting its new cabins and spa. Consider national newspaper advertising, a travel trade fair, or social media influencer marketing. Which should LEI choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National newspaper advertising: Print adverts in national newspapers could reach a wide, affluent readership and build awareness of the new lakeside cabins and spa quickly. However, national rates are expensive for a company spending $720,000 on the build, and many readers live too far away to book a $55.00 room-night, so response could be low and spend wasted.

Travel trade fair: A trade fair lets LEI meet tour operators and travel agents face to face, generating bookings and useful feedback on the 63% of guests drawn by the lakeside location. It is focused and relationship-building, but it is costly in stand fees and staff time, reaches only industry buyers rather than the 72% of surveyed guests who would return directly, and produces fewer immediate consumer bookings.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and lifestyle influencers can show the cabins and spa to exactly the guests who value the lakeside setting, with the 380-person survey showing 72% would return and 63% care most about location. Engagement is measurable and cost per lead is low, though results take time and depend on choosing credible influencers.

Recommendation: LEI should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the segment the research identified, costs far less than national print and reaches individual guests a trade fair cannot, while showcasing the new $720,000 cabins. Newspapers are rejected as expensive and untargeted; the trade fair is rejected as slow and buyer-focused rather than filling rooms directly. The 72% return rate suggests keeping existing guests engaged matters more than expensive mass reach, reinforcing the low-cost digital option. Influencer content can also highlight the lakeside location that 63% of respondents value, which a newspaper advert cannot demonstrate as vividly.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of LEI with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of LEI with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspapers and the trade fair are rejected.

questions.question_text: Cleanliness complaints at LEI have risen to 34 a month. Explain two benefits for LEI of using laissez-faire leadership to improve service quality.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives LEI's experienced inn managers freedom to solve cleanliness problems in their own way, which can produce quick, local fixes to the 34 monthly complaints without waiting for head office. With a flat organisational structure and only 52 staff, this autonomy uses the knowledge of managers closest to housekeeping and protects the 78% occupancy rate and the $55.00 room price.

Point 2: Delegating decisions can motivate skilled managers and support the 72% of surveyed guests who would return, because teams can tailor service to the 63% who book for the lakeside location. Freed from constant approval steps, managers can schedule the $540 housekeeping retraining promptly, helping reduce complaints and staff turnover while the $720,000 cabins and spa open. With 4,800 room-nights sold last quarter and 72% likely to return, letting managers fix service locally protects the revenue that funds the $720,000 cabins. Delegation also uses the flat structure to respond faster than a centralised team could when cleanliness complaints reach 34 a month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to LEI's complaints, occupancy and service quality.

questions.question_text: LEI must improve housekeeping standards. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local hospitality college. Which should LEI choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching housekeeping staff in LEI's own rooms is directly relevant to the cleanliness standards behind the 34 monthly complaints, costs no fees and keeps the 52 staff productive while they learn, protecting 78% occupancy and the survey's 72% return rate. The drawback is that trainers are working staff with less time for rooms, bad habits may be copied, and there is no certificate to prove standards to guests.

Off-the-job training: The local hospitality college offers structured housekeeping methods and a recognised qualification at $540 per employee, which could lift service quality and justify the $55.00 price. However, it removes staff from the inn, reducing room-turnover capacity during the cabins and spa launch, and generic content may not match LEI's exact checklists, so on-site follow-up would be needed.

Decision: LEI should choose on-the-job training as the main approach, with short college accreditation for senior housekeepers. It is cheaper, specific to LEI's rooms and avoids losing room capacity while complaints stand at 34 a month. Full off-the-job training is rejected because sending many staff away would disrupt occupancy and add $540-per-person fees on top of a $720,000 investment; college modules can follow once standards rise. Since 63% of guests book for the lakeside location rather than staff credentials, the safest immediate fix is on-site coaching at $540 per person. Full college training would remove housekeepers when occupancy is 78%, risking room-turnover delays and further complaints during the $720,000 launch. Senior housekeepers can then cascade the standards to the rest of the 52 staff once the cabins open.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to LEI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of LEI.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of LEI with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how LEI's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($55.00 − $30.00) = $240,000 ÷ $25.00 = 9,600 units. Answer: break-even output is 9,600 guest-room-night units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $55.00 − $30.00 = $25.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $25.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways LEI's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 9,600-unit break-even output with actual output of 18,000 room-nights to confirm the inns are profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 8,400 room-nights before the new cabins are essential.
2. Contribution per unit of $25.00 lets LEI test a midweek discount on the $55.00 price; managers can judge how many extra room-nights are needed to still cover the $240,000 fixed costs.
3. The break-even figure helps plan the $320,000 loan interest and returns to the $400,000 share issue, checking that 18,000 room-nights generate enough contribution before further funding the $720,000 expansion.
4. Average total cost of $43.33 a unit ($240,000 ÷ 18,000 + $30.00) can be benchmarked against 78% occupancy and the 34 monthly cleanliness complaints, guiding the $540 retraining spend as energy and laundry costs rise 10.2%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 9,600 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $25.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 18,000 room-nights; discount modelling on the $55.00 price; loan and share-issue planning for the $720,000 expansion; and average total cost benchmarking at $43.33 to tackle complaints.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LEI's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has LEI's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.45 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.52 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $45,000 inventories + $75,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $145,000; 2025 current assets = $40,000 + $90,000 + $70,000 = $200,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $145,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.45 and 2025 = $200,000 ÷ $105,000 = 1.90. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($145,000 − $45,000) ÷ $100,000 = 1.00 and 2025 = ($200,000 − $40,000) ÷ $105,000 = 1.52.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The 2024 figure of 1.45 rose to 1.90 as cash nearly tripled from $25,000 to $70,000 while current liabilities edged up only from $100,000 to $105,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, improved from 1.00 to 1.52, so LEI can meet short-term debts without relying on stock — helpful while it services a $320,000 loan and spends $720,000 on cabins and a spa. However, trade receivables rose from $75,000 to $90,000, tying up cash, so the stronger position depends partly on guests and agents paying on time.

Conclusion: LEI's financial position has improved. Both measures rose (1.45 to 1.90 and 1.00 to 1.52) and the cash build means the improvement is not inventory-driven. The residual risk is growing receivables, so LEI should keep tight credit control while funding the expansion. The stronger position gives LEI capacity to absorb the 10.2% energy and laundry inflation without delaying the $720,000 build. Continued cash discipline on the $90,000 of receivables will help keep both measures above their 1.45 and 1.00 starting levels.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether LEI's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for LEI of introducing energy-saving measures in its inns.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Cutting energy use directly offsets the 10.2% rise in energy and laundry costs and reduces the $30.00 variable cost per guest-room night, protecting the $25.00 contribution and the $55.00 price. With occupancy at 78% and 72% of surveyed guests likely to return, greener inns can strengthen the lakeside brand and help justify the $720,000 cabins and spa investment.

Disadvantage: Installing efficient equipment needs upfront spending that adds to fixed costs of $240,000 a year, on top of a $320,000 loan and the $720,000 build. If occupancy falls below 78%, the savings may not repay the outlay quickly, and any disruption during installation could worsen the 34 monthly cleanliness complaints and the high housekeeping turnover. If efficiency equipment is not installed, the 10.2% cost rise will push the $30.00 variable cost higher and squeeze the $25.00 contribution. With 72% of guests likely to return, LEI has a chance to protect the $55.00 price, but only if the savings are real.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to LEI's costs, occupancy and survey data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in energy and laundry costs will affect LEI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.75%): If LEI's $320,000 loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by 1.25% of $320,000 = $4,000. That is modest beside fixed costs of $240,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is nil. Higher rates could still dampen demand for weekend breaks, but LEI can cap the exposure by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.04 per hour): With a workforce of 52, most housekeeping and service roles are hourly-paid, so the rise feeds into the wage bill. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the fair comparison is the given output of 18,000 room-nights across 52 staff, about 346 room-nights per worker. If productivity holds and the $540 retraining reduces the 34 complaints, the $25.00 contribution can absorb it; if turnover persists, unit labour cost rises.

Energy and laundry inflation (10.2%): The $30.00 variable cost per unit is where these costs sit, but the insert gives no breakdown, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole $30.00 rose 10.2%, that is 0.102 × $30.00 = $3.06 per unit, about $55,080 a year at 18,000 room-nights. Even a $2.00-per-unit rise costs $36,000 a year, cutting contribution from $25.00 toward $23.00.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in energy and laundry costs will have the greatest impact because it recurs on every room-night and erodes the $25.00 contribution funding the $720,000 expansion. The wage rise is significant but manageable if productivity holds, while the interest rise adds only about $4,000.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to LEI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on LEI's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of LEI with a well-justified judgment that energy and laundry inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
